name: ALG1-CDG (CDG-Ik)
aliases: congenital disorder of glycosylation type Ik

reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: An N-linked type I congenital disorder of glycosylation caused by biallelic ALG1 variants impairing early assembly of the lipid-linked oligosaccharide on dolichol
Typically a severe multisystem paediatric disorder with profound developmental delay, hypotonia, drug-resistant epilepsy and frequent early mortality
Systemic features overlap the broader CDG phenotype: hepatopathy, coagulopathy with low antithrombin and factor levels, and endocrine abnormalities
Nephrotic-range proteinuria, hydrops and oedema are reported and reflect impaired glycosylation of plasma and structural proteins
Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing shows a type I pattern (increased asialo- and disialotransferrin) reflecting under-occupancy of N-glycan sites
There is no disease-specific pharmacotherapy; management is supportive and multidisciplinary, coordinated through a metabolic service
Diagnosis is confirmed by ALG1 molecular genetic testing after a suggestive transferrin pattern
reference.pathophysiology: ALG1 encodes a mannosyltransferase that adds the first mannose to the growing dolichol-linked oligosaccharide within the endoplasmic reticulum. Loss of function truncates assembly of the lipid-linked precursor, so fewer complete oligosaccharides are transferred en bloc to nascent proteins, producing under-glycosylation at N-linked sites. Because the defect lies in assembly and transfer of the precursor rather than its later trimming, the biochemical signature is a type I transferrin pattern. Widespread hypoglycosylation of enzymes, transport proteins, clotting factors and membrane receptors underlies the multisystem paediatric phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Other N-linked type I CDG subtypes (e.g. PMM2-CDG, ALG3-CDG, ALG12-CDG)
Early-onset epileptic encephalopathies of other genetic causes
Congenital muscular dystrophies with brain involvement
Non-glycosylation causes of neonatal hydrops or nephrotic syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing or mass spectrometry to identify a type I glycosylation pattern
ALG1 molecular genetic (gene panel or exome) confirmation
Coagulation studies including antithrombin, protein C, factor XI and factor IX
Liver function tests and abdominal imaging for hepatopathy
Neuroimaging and electroencephalography for encephalopathy and seizures
redFlags: Neonatal or infantile hydrops, generalised oedema or nephrotic-range proteinuria
Bleeding or thrombotic events from combined coagulation factor deficiency
Failure to thrive with multi-organ involvement suggesting a severe CDG
reference.prognosis: ALG1-CDG is among the more severe glycosylation disorders, and many affected infants die in the first years of life; survivors typically have profound neurodevelopmental disability. Prognosis correlates broadly with residual enzyme activity and the burden of systemic complications.
pitfalls: Attributing the transferrin abnormality to secondary causes such as galactosaemia, alcohol or sepsis without confirmatory genetics
Overlooking the coagulopathy, which can cause both bleeding and thrombosis
Expecting a disease-modifying pharmacological treatment when only supportive care exists
Missing the diagnosis when a normal transferrin pattern occurs, as some CDG subtypes can screen falsely negative
references: Scriver's OMMBID, congenital disorders of glycosylation
Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics, inborn errors of metabolism
